newsitem.title: PORTUGAL: FEATURE - Taking the bull by the horns, Portuguese style.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Taking the bull by the horns, Portuguese style.

text.p: Goading a 500-kilo (1,100-lb) fighting bull into charging and then trying to wrestle it to a halt is not be everybody's idea of fun.
But that is what Goncalo da Cunha Ferreira and his fellow "forcados" do numerous times during the Portuguese bullfighting season between April and October.
The forcados -- from the Portuguese word for pitchfork -- are an intergral part of a local "corrida' (bullfight) but unlike bullfighters, they receive no pay and don't want to.
They do it for love of the thrill and tradition.

Cunha Ferreira, a property consultant when away from the bullring, is the chief of the Forcados de Santarem, one of the largest and most renowned of the groups, which is in demand most weeks during the six-month season.

The forcados are unique to Portuguese corridas where, unlike in Spain, Mexico and parts of Latin America, the bulls are not killed in the ring. Another difference is that most bullfighters -- at least the most prestigious -- do their fighting mounted on a horse.

The forcados enter the sandy arena after the bull has been "fought" by the horseman -- known as a cavaleiro -- and their task is to subdue the angry animal with nothing but their bodies and bare hands.
"It is pretty dangerous but the better prepared you are physically and psychologically, the less risky it is," said 29-year-old Cunha Ferreira, who has been part of the Santarem team since he was 17.

The fact that bulls are not killed in the ring -- it was banned in 1799 -- means that the drama at a Portuguese bullfight is generated by the horsemanship of the cavaleiros, dashingly attired in 18th century jacket and breeches, and the gritty courage of the forcados.
The forcados work only with the cavaleiros. Although bulls are also fought on foot in Portugal, the foot-bound "toureiros' have never enjoyed the same status as in Spain.

The forcados were employed originally to prevent the bulls from getting too close to distinguished onlookers by using wooden, two-pronged pitchforks which locked onto the bulls' horns, Cunha Ferreira said.
They gradually became part of the show, even if the techniques and discipline that now regulate their performance were developed only during this century.
The forcado team, with its uniform of small brown jacket and kneebreeches, is made up of eight members, each of whom has a specific role in subduing the bull.
But it is the man at the front of the line that takes most of the kudos as well as most of the knocks.
Edging to within 10 or 15 yards (metres) of the bull, still panting from its exertions in chasing the horse, the lead forcado seeks to rouse it into a fresh charge.
When the bull obliges, the forcado takes the blow in the midriff, wraps his arms around the bull's horns and seeks to hang on for dear life as his team rushes to help.
Surprisingly, they usually succeed in bringing the bull to a halt, although it can take several hair-raising attempts.
Equally surprisingly, there have been few fatalities -- the last was five years ago -- although broken bones and bruising are pretty common.
"You try to reduce the risk but still it is inexplicable really that there are not more injuries," Cunha Ferreira said.
He was seriously hurt in 1988 when he was tossed into the air by a bull and landed on his neck.
He was out of the ring for two years but returned as soon as the doctors gave him the all-clear.
"It happened when things were going very well for me and I was full of confidence...if it had been now I would probably call it a day," he said.

The forcados are a proud and closely-knit bunch. While they are not slow to criticise fight organisers for tightfistedness when it comes to providing hotels and meals, nobody wants to be formally paid.
"It is a question of personal pride...we are people who like to run risks and overcome them," said Cunha Ferreira.
There are other rewards. "We get nothing but the applause of the crowd, good dinners and pretty women," he said.
